title: The Cow Tail Switch
text:
A West African tale tells of a hunter named Ogaloussa who went into the forest one day and did not come back. Weeks passed. His family went on with their lives, and his sons stopped speaking of him.

Then a son was born to his wife. When the child began to talk, his first words were, "Where is my father?" The eldest son said they should look for him. The brothers went into the forest and each used his own gift. One knew how to find the path, and he led them to the place where their father had been killed and only his bones remained. One knew how to put bones together, and he assembled the skeleton. One restored the sinews, another the blood, another the flesh, another the breath. At last Ogaloussa sat up and walked home with them.

Later Ogaloussa made a beautiful switch from a cow's tail, the finest object of its kind, and announced that he would give it to the son who had done the most to bring him back. The brothers each argued their case.

Ogaloussa gave it to the baby. A man is not truly dead, he said, until he is forgotten. The one who asked "Where is my father?" was the one who brought him home.
lesson: Remembering and asking after the absent is itself a form of care. In families, the one who keeps asking is often the one who holds everyone together.
source: Harold Courlander and George Herzog, The Cow-Tail Switch and Other West African Stories (1947)
